build: Software Projects disk, alternate D64 with LA–LJ files

exclude: Live main screen and sprite pointers. The clear routine at $15EF writes this matrix.
Embedded first-descent source, copied to $1E00 and decoded to $4000. The second descent reads its graphics stream again.
9 parts: Phantom Knight, First falling platform, Burning Ropes and others
10 parts: Burning Ropes, First falling platform, Skull Hallway and others
extra: Resident snapshot bytes beyond the first scene even where other scenes later overwrite them
Bytes beneath VIC registers preceding the embedded scene
elsewhere: 9 parts: Phantom Knight, First falling platform, Burning Ropes and others
10 parts: Burning Ropes, First falling platform, Skull Hallway and others

comments.text: Add $40 to A to form the filename suffix after the fixed L at $039C. Blank the screen and save the processor port, VIC interrupt state and tape/serial flag, then call SETLFS for device 8, secondary 1, SETNAM and LOAD. Restore the saved state and enable interrupts after the load.
Two PETSCII bytes passed to SETNAM. The loader writes the second byte before each request.
Disable interrupts while waiting for the high raster bit in $D011, then leave with interrupts enabled.
The first 64 eight-byte character glyphs selected by the interstitial VIC setup at $10A8. They include the blank tile and the illustrated castle wall cells.
Twelve glyphs for screen codes $40–$4B, between the castle tile group and the digit glyphs. The interstitial writes codes $43, $4A and $4B directly at $11BA–$11C5.
Ten eight-byte glyphs in digit order 0 through 9. The copier at $1880 writes them to character codes $B0–$B9 when A is $78.
Characters $56–$5F follow the decimal digits. The interstitial draws character $56 for the lit markers along the top of the castle screen.
Characters $60–$7F contain the castle display alphabet. The high-score heading at $1307 masks each letter to five bits and adds $60 to select a glyph.
Reset the sound player, seed state from CIA1 timer A, set the score display pointers, bank out the ROMs, and set up the game interrupt vectors before entering the attract flow.
Reset the stack to $DF, clear the sprite high-X register and call the unpacked scene entry at $1E01. For nonzero scenes clear $23 first.

Disable all sprites. On a successful scene (nonzero $25), increment $26 and load that scene. Starting at scene index 4, increment $27 when it is below 4. A zero outcome instead calls $12D8 and restarts at $0C00.
Pass the next scene number in $26 to the disk loader, then enter the inter-scene path at $1D00.
Draw the eleven-cell fire prompt, wait for a CIA2 timer event, then poll port 2 fire at $DC00 bit 4. Restore SID volume to 15 and unpack the scene before returning to the shared caller.
Reset the scene index to zero and set the source pointer to the boot payload at $D010 and its copy destination to $1E00. Pick the first escape byte from $1CBA and invoke the shared unpacker.
Clear the tape-port state and set CIA1 port A to $7F. Poll active-low bit 4 on CIA1 port B before returning.
Clear the message screen, convert 31 bytes from $1C4B to six-bit screen codes and display them with colour 7. Then call the port 1 fire wait.
Set CIA1 port A to $7F and poll bit 4 of port B until the active-low fire input is asserted.
Clear screen page $0400 and its colours, select VIC bank zero and program $D018=$15 before returning.

Compare the scene identifier at $8010 against the requested index at $26. If they differ fall back to $0D2A. Otherwise use the requested number to look up the escape byte and unpack from $8010 to $1E00.

Blank the display, install the shared raster handler, and copy bytes to $1E00 while looking for the eleven-byte marker at $1C40. Read input with I/O banked out, then use the page after the marker as the graphics stream and start output at $4000.
Temporarily map RAM under I/O, read the next source byte through $2A/$2B, restore I/O and copy the byte through $2C/$2D. X counts consecutive matching bytes of END OF CODE.

Copy ordinary bytes to the graphics destination. An escape byte introduces a repeated value and an eight-bit count, where zero yields up to 256 stores. Stop at the destination limit in $03EC/$03ED even inside a run.
Compare the output pointer with the exclusive limit. Continue decoding below it. At the limit set the screen page and palette for the shared colour routine, then re-enable the screen.
Clear bitmap and display-enable bits in $D011 and force the raster compare high bit to zero.
Set the display-enable bit, 25-row selection and low scroll bits in $D011, with raster compare below line 256.
Clear twelve successive bytes beginning at $03B0, including the three-byte packed BCD score.

Clear the sound effect requests and score, then draw the castle. Animate the alternate sprite setup and decrement the attempt counter. On zero display the failure message and return to the caller using the saved stack. Otherwise finish the interstitial and return to the scene restart path.
Reverse the horizontal motion, bring the sprites toward their saved positions and alternate the castle and partial sprite setups. Hide the sprites and release the score service gate before returning.
Pace one sprite selected by $03D8, update horizontal motion inside its allowed Y range and change Y according to its vertical direction.
Move the indexed sprite toward the saved coordinates at $44 and decrement Y while it differs from the saved position.
Add or subtract two from the selected sprite low X. At the changeover thresholds flip the direction and update the vertical state.
Call the CIA2 delay and decrement X until it reaches zero.
Count down from the incoming Y value, then repeat a full eight-bit countdown. Both loops decrement Y and use X to count two passes.

Select character display in VIC bank zero with screen at $0400. Clear the display, fill nine pairs of brick rows from the alternating tables at $1B24/$1B28, set their colours and copy the decorative cell rows.
Install the coordinates, pointers and expansion masks for sprites 0–3 from $1C12 through $1C1F.
Install the coordinates, pointers and expansion masks for sprites 0–3 from $1C04 through $1C11.
Write the position and high-X register from the table at $1BC6, then install eight colours and sprite pointers from $1BDF and $1BD7. Set the X and Y expansion masks.
Install the alternate coordinates, frame pointers and expansion masks for all eight sprites. Save the starting coordinate and direction bytes for the animation.
Draw up to five lit marker cells at $0411–$0415 from the count in $27. A matching slot receives glyph $56 and colour 1, then the count is decremented for the next slot.
Set up the score display, request sound $82 and try to insert the score. Carry set skips the subsequent presentation.
Set up the score display again, select sound $8B, draw the rows and call the delay with X=$7D before the fade at $1778.
Draw the castle interstitial and high-score rows before disabling all sprites.
Write the high-score heading and five 11-character rows in screen RAM, using a different character-code mapping for the initials and points. Set the colour RAM for both areas.
Compare five new score digits with each table entry and find where the new score outranks a row. Shift 11-byte rows down, copy in the score and prepare the on-screen initials field.
Call the timer wait with X equal to 3, then fall through to the initials editor poll.

Poll joystick port 2 in up, down, left, right, fire order. Up and down cycle the character between $60 and $7A. Left and right wrap the cursor over three initials. The idle loop increments the selected cell's colour and fire exits the editor.
Multiply the saved row index in $0D by eleven and add $1518 to form the row pointer in $2A/$2B. Put the following row's address in $2C/$2D and return with carry clear.
The ENEMIES OF THE DRAGON heading. $1307 maps its letters into the colour title alphabet.
Five 11-byte high-score rows displayed from $131C. The insertion routine at $139A shifts rows and writes into this area.
The descending copy at $13E8–$13EA shifts the previous fifth score row from $1544 here, into eleven bytes at $154F–$1559. A zero byte follows before the initializer at $155B.
Fill sixteen character slots beginning at $03BC with screen code $B0, the score digit zero.
Preserve A, increment the byte at $156F and acknowledge CIA2 through $DD0D before returning from the interrupt.
The NMI at $1566 increments this byte. The wait at $1625 compares it against the value sampled before the timer starts.
Wait for the lower part of the frame, then point $42/$43 to $16A7, set raster compare to $A0 and clear its high bit.
Jump to the raster-high wait at $039F.
A BPL with displacement $FB targets $1589, then an RTS follows. The JMP at $1589 replaces the fall-through entry to this fragment.
A jump to the port 2 sampler at $1592.
Write $FF to CIA1 port A, latch the port value into $28, and restore $7F to the CIA port. The joystick pulls pressed bits low.
Jump to the timer setup and NMI-counter wait at $1625.
Set the period count to two, load CIA2 timer A with $5801 and poll its interrupt register. Decrement the count after each event.
Use A as the upper byte of CIA2 timer A, set the repeat count to one and share the polling loop with the two-period wait.
Save A, X and Y to the three zero-page locations starting at $0A.
Jump to the shared CIA2 NMI-counter wait without pushing another return address.
Reload A, X and Y from the scratch slots beginning at $0A.
Treat A as the screen page and clear four pages there and four pages of colour RAM starting at $D800.
Jump into the CIA2 tick wait immediately before the between-scenes fire poll.
Use $23 to select the state of processor-port bit 5, keeping the data direction register at $2F.
Return from the polling delay immediately before the NMI-counter-based wait at $1625.
Enable CIA2 timer A interrupts, start the timer, write $010A to its latch, and wait for the NMI counter at $156F to change before clearing the CIA2 interrupt mask.
Save the registers and clear decimal mode. For VIC raster IRQs acknowledge bit 0 and dispatch indirectly through $42/$43. Otherwise restore the registers and return with RTI.
Pull Y, X and A from the stack in order, then return from the interrupt.
Read four pages of screen cell indices from the page named in $03D6. Look each one up in the table at the address patched into $1678 and write the result to colour RAM.
A one-byte $EA between the colour copy return and the product routine at $168A.
Multiply the unsigned bytes in $05 and $06 with eight shift-and-add iterations, shifting $06 down to zero and returning the result in $07/$08.
Advance the resident sound service, then use the common IRQ exit at $165B.

Use the pointer in A to find its 64-byte sprite record in the bank at $4000. If byte 63 differs from $03EF, update the orientation marker and reverse the 24 bits in each of the 21 rows. Return with A, X and Y restored.
Swap the first and third bytes of the next row and reverse all eight bits of each byte before the three stores.
Use the two nibble tables at $1B04 and $1B14 to reverse the eight bits in A, leaving an all-zero or all-one byte unchanged.
Fill five seed bytes at $03CC from CIA1 timer A low, then force the high bits of the fifth byte into the range $20 through $E0. The following entry doubles and advances the seed.
Constrain the fifth seed byte, double the five-byte seed into $03D1 and add it back to the seed. Add a second contribution to the low three bytes and return the new low byte.
Request sound $88 through $C000 and call $1083 with X=$50.
Call $17AF, advance the sound player at $C004, then service the processor port at $1601.
Add A to the three-byte packed-decimal score at $03B0–$03B2 with carry propagation, leaving decimal mode clear.
Skip the score countdown while its gate or update lock is set. Otherwise choose a BCD decrement from the score's middle byte and subtract it with borrow.
Clear $1B03 and return so future interrupt service can update the score.
Set X to five and add $99 to the packed BCD score on each iteration of the shared loop.
Set X to three and enter the shared repeated BCD addition.
Set X to two and enter the shared repeated BCD addition.
Set X to one and enter the shared addition of $99 to the packed BCD score.
For each of 80 bytes, copy the score glyph at $0A60 plus Y to the address from A plus five pages and offset $80.
Clear sound requests at $C001 and $C002 and write cue $89 to $C000.
Clear sprite priority, multicolour and expansion masks. Clear the bitmap and raster high bits and keep only the low four bits of $D016.
The $02 byte separates the VIC mode routine return at $18CA from the attract setup at $18CC. Executing $02 as an NMOS 6502 opcode would halt the CPU.
Prepare the attract display, request music $80, and place the thirteen title characters at screen position $072D with colour 7.
Use $03F3 to choose an attract message. When $1CC4 is nonzero, also recolour the eleven-character fire prompt from the random generator and set a shorter display interval.
The thirteen title characters rendered in the attract display by $18D6.
The attract text selector at $1948 points here. The renderer reads column 8 before the programming credit text.
Programming credit for John Darnell.
The high-bit $FF ends the programming credit. The next byte, column 6, introduces the final screen credit.
Credit for final screen by Steve Birtles.
The high-bit $FF ends the final screen credit. Column 5 follows as the starting cell for the sound credit.
Credit for music and sound by Colin Porch.
The sound credit ends at $FF. The graphics credit begins at the column in the next byte, 4.
Credit for graphics drawn by Nicole Baikaloff.
A high-bit terminator ends the graphics credit. The next byte starts the fire prompt at column 11.
Message telling the player to press fire to start.
The fire prompt terminates here. The next byte starts the publisher line at column 5.
Software Projects presenter credit.
The publisher credit terminates at $FF. The selector at $193C points to the following byte, column 7 for the score prompt.
Message telling the player to press space for the high score.
A high-bit $FF ends the score prompt and takes the renderer branch at $19A1 before the failure message.
Failure message about the attempt to rescue Princess Daphne.
A PETSCII red control byte and space follow the failure text, before the next-scene prompt. The two failure display rows use fixed-width glyph reads.
Eleven prompt characters loaded by $0CE1.
Gate tested by the score service at $17AF. The failure interstitial sets it and clears it on exit.
Reversed bit patterns for the upper input nibble, returned in the lower output nibble.
Reversed bit patterns for the lower input nibble, returned in the upper output nibble.
Two four-character row patterns for the castle background. The loop at $10D6 subtracts $41 from each source byte, repeats the pattern across 40 cells and alternates the starting phase.
The first seven rows of thirteen decoration cells for the inset beginning at $045D. A zero writes a blank and a nonzero byte is translated by subtracting $41.
The eighth decoration row, repeated for another eight rows by the loop at $116D.
Forty translated character codes for the row at $06D0. Translated codes $3C or above receive colour 1.
Ten translated character codes written into the next row starting at $06FA.
Initial values copied to $D000–$D010 by the interstitial sprite setup.
Eight initial VIC sprite pointers copied to $07F8–$07FF at $125F.
Eight initial sprite colours copied to $D027–$D02E at $1259.
Two initial masks written to $D01D and $D017 after the sprite setup.
Seventeen VIC position and high X values installed by the alternate interstitial sprite setup.
Pointers for eight sprite slots on the failure interstitial. The installer at $1293 copies them to $07F8.
Horizontal and vertical expansion masks for the full alternate sprite setup at $1272.
Eight coordinates, four frame pointers and two expansion masks installed by $1212.
Eight coordinates, four frame pointers and two expansion masks installed by $11E6.
Initial horizontal movement signs for the eight sprites. The interstitial animator changes the sign at its limits.
Initial vertical movement signs for the eight sprites copied to $03E1 by the alternate setup.
One mask per VIC sprite to test a collision latch or set a bit in a sprite control register.
The inverse masks for clearing the indexed sprite bit without touching the other sprites.
Eleven bytes spelling END OF CODE. The unpacker copies through this marker and starts decoding picture bytes at the next page.
Messages about pressing play and space and rewinding the tape, following the code delimiter.
One escape byte per scene, indexed by $26. A match in the compressed picture stream changes the two following bytes from literals to value and run length.
The tenth escape-table byte is $0F. If the header comparison accepts selector 9, $0DC6 reads this slot and $0DC9 stores it in $03EE.
The attract screen tests this counter at $18EE to choose its flashing fire prompt. Fire decrements it at $19E0.
A fragment of the Burning Ropes path through the later thresholds. These bytes match the room code at $25A0–$25D9, beginning inside an instruction.
Call $1093 and $123E to prepare the inter-scene display, request sound $87 and jump into the fire wait at $0CDF.

Retained bytes immediately after the replacement inter-scene jump. The fragment contains the same LDA #$0C, STA $2F28 and JMP $27D4 as the Burning Ropes approach at $25E9, with the two bytes $17 $0E inserted before the jump. The final JSR targets $1819 here and $1871 in the room.
A retained Burning Ropes instruction fragment matching $25F3–$2655, including the approach countdown and action test.
Low operand byte $19 of a retained JSR. It differs from the operand at the equivalent Burning Ropes address $2656, where the low byte is $71.
A retained Burning Ropes instruction fragment matching $2657–$26BB. It covers the last approach countdown and its action path.
Low operand byte $19 of a retained JSR. It differs from the operand at the equivalent Burning Ropes address $26BC, where the low byte is $71.
A retained Burning Ropes instruction fragment matching $26BD–$26D7. It includes a sound request and sprite coordinate stores.
Second-descent tail fragment beginning with the branch displacement of the countdown at $2F56, followed by enabling sprites 0–3 and returning.
A copy of the second-descent sprite alignment routine. It sets the four low X coordinates alike and gives sprites 2 and 3 a Y coordinate $15 below sprite 0.
The END OF CODE delimiter copied at the end of the second-descent record.
A single $EA after the resident copy of the second-descent delimiter and before the retained Tentacle Room overlay bytes.
Tail of the Tentacle Room 18-byte sprite overlay records, from the colour fields in record 4 through the last record.
The END OF CODE delimiter that follows the Tentacle Room overlay records.
The $EA after the resident copy of the Tentacle Room delimiter, before the retained Weapons Room overlay bytes.
Tail of the Weapons Room 18-byte sprite overlay records, beginning at byte 3 of record 1.
The Weapons Room cell animation state, eight screen cell pointers and the associated character codes.
The Weapons Room raster band index, then the projectile frame pointers, coordinate pairs and high-X masks.
The Weapons Room timing counters and projectile motion initialization record.
Resident copy of the seven six-character rows used by the Weapons Room sequence at $26DE. The first row uses five characters and the following six use all six.
The eleven-character END OF CODE signature follows the retained Weapons Room screen patch. The scene loader checks this signature to find the picture stream page.
A single $EA after the retained Weapons Room delimiter and before the colour bytes at $31E1.
A copy of the LB packed colour-lookup tokens at $A099–$A0B7. They expand to the Burning Ropes character colours for indices $01–$20 at $7701–$7720, including the four-cell run at $7708.
Ninety authored bytes copied in descending index order to $44–$9D by the Skull Hallway initialization loop at $1E70.
Pose record $01 for the shared character raster multiplexer. The scene copies 90 bytes to $44–$9D. The first raster band selects sprite pointers $00, $00, $00.
Pose record $02 for the shared character raster multiplexer. The scene copies 90 bytes to $44–$9D. The first raster band selects sprite pointers $90, $22, $1F.
Pose record $03 for the shared character raster multiplexer. The scene copies 90 bytes to $44–$9D. The first raster band selects sprite pointers $00, $00, $00.

Pose record $0A for the shared character raster multiplexer. The scene copies 90 bytes to $44–$9D. The first raster band selects sprite pointers $00, $00, $00.

Pose record $10 for the shared character raster multiplexer. The scene copies 90 bytes to $44–$9D. The first raster band selects sprite pointers $00, $00, $00.

Zero-run encoded character cells for the tail of the first descent ending matrix at $4CE1–$4F94. A nonzero byte is a literal cell. A zero byte introduces one byte giving the number of consecutive blank cells.
Eight 64-byte castle-animation sprite records addressed by pointers $E8–$EF in the table at $1BFA. The installer selects them for the eight moving pieces.
64-byte source for interstitial sprite 0. The setup at $125F puts pointer $F0 into its entry of the $0400 screen matrix.
64-byte source for interstitial sprite 1. The setup at $125F puts pointer $F1 into its entry of the $0400 screen matrix.
64-byte source for interstitial sprite 2. The setup at $125F puts pointer $F2 into its entry of the $0400 screen matrix.
64-byte source for interstitial sprite 7. The setup at $125F puts pointer $F3 into its entry of the $0400 screen matrix.
64-byte source for interstitial sprite 4. The setup at $125F puts pointer $F4 into its entry of the $0400 screen matrix.
64-byte source for interstitial sprite 5. The setup at $125F puts pointer $F5 into its entry of the $0400 screen matrix.
64-byte source for interstitial sprite 3. The setup at $125F puts pointer $F6 into its entry of the $0400 screen matrix.
64-byte source for interstitial sprite 6. The setup at $125F puts pointer $F7 into its entry of the $0400 screen matrix.
Four 64-byte sprite records used by the partial setup at $1212. The table at $1C0C assigns these frames to sprites 0–3.
Four 64-byte sprite records used by the partial setup at $11E6. The table at $1C1A assigns these frames to sprites 0–3.
Three pending sound request bytes. The following byte at $C003 is the logical channel index reset by the sound driver at $C006.

Copy each of five channel state records into zero page, select a request byte, call the channel player and copy the changed records back. Clear the high bit of the three request slots after processing the channels.

Service the selected logical channel, then save four updated channel bytes into its work record. After all five records, clear the retrigger bits on the first three cue requests and write the voice-one register buffer or clear its gate.
Choose the buffer at $CF or $DD according to the cue in $C001. If the selected frequency high byte is zero, clear gate at $D40B. The alternate-buffer gate-clear path returns immediately.

Choose the buffer at $D6 or $E4 according to the cue in $C002. Write seven registers starting at $D40E when the frequency high byte is nonzero, otherwise write the selected control byte with gate cleared.

Select the channel cue and pattern tables. A request with bit 7 set begins a cue. Otherwise count down the current note, clear gate at count 2, and interpret the next pattern command when the count reaches zero.
Read the cue repeat count and pattern index and load the pattern pointer. A high-bit terminator restarts the sequence for channels 0–2 or clears the corresponding request for channels 3–4.
Mask the command to an instrument index, multiply by five and copy the five pulse, control and envelope settings to the channel register buffer.
Load the duration and advance the pattern cursor. Translate the note index through the two frequency tables, then set the gate bit in the buffered control register.
Clear the SID register range through $D41C, two request bytes and the player scratch variables.
The low bytes of the five cue lookup table addresses, loaded by $C0D3 when X selects a logical channel.
The high bytes of the five cue lookup table addresses, loaded by $C0D3 when X selects a logical channel.
The low bytes of each channel register buffer pointer, loaded by $C0D3 when X selects a logical channel.
The high bytes of each channel register buffer pointer, loaded by $C0D3 when X selects a logical channel.
The low bytes of the five pattern pointer table addresses, loaded by $C0D3 when X selects a logical channel.
The high bytes of the five pattern pointer table addresses, loaded by $C0D3 when X selects a logical channel.
Five four-byte working records, holding cue pointer and pattern pointer for each channel. The sound service loads and stores these around the per-channel interpreter.
42 five-byte instrument records. The low six bits of a pattern command with bit 7 set and bit 6 clear select pulse low, pulse high, control, attack/decay and sustain/release.
Cue pointers for logical sound channel 0. A request with bit 7 set indexes this list with its low seven bits. A zero pointer has no score.
Cue pointers for logical sound channel 1. A request with bit 7 set indexes this list with its low seven bits. A zero pointer has no score.
Cue pointers for logical sound channel 2. A request with bit 7 set indexes this list with its low seven bits. A zero pointer has no score.
Cue pointers for logical sound channel 3. A request with bit 7 set indexes this list with its low seven bits. A zero pointer has no score.
Cue pointers for logical sound channel 4. A request with bit 7 set indexes this list with its low seven bits. A zero pointer has no score.
Cue sequence at $C354, used by channel/cue 0/12. Repeat count and pattern index pairs: 1×27, 127×23. The high-bit byte ends the sequence.
Cue sequence at $C359, used by channel/cue 1/12. Repeat count and pattern index pairs: 1×22, 127×11. The high-bit byte ends the sequence.

SID pattern at $C35E, selected by channel/pattern 0/27. Contains 10 note-duration pairs and 1 inline instrument selections. At the final opcode the interpreter repeats the pattern while repetitions remain. Otherwise it advances to the next cue pair.

SID pattern at $C374, selected by channel/pattern 1/22. Contains 10 note-duration pairs and 1 inline instrument selections. At the final opcode the interpreter repeats the pattern while repetitions remain. Otherwise it advances to the next cue pair.
Cue sequence at $C38A, used by channel/cue 3/7. Repeat count and pattern index pairs: 1×7. The high-bit byte ends the sequence.
Cue sequence at $C38D, used by channel/cue 3/8. Repeat count and pattern index pairs: 1×8. The high-bit byte ends the sequence.

SID pattern at $C390, selected by channel/pattern 3/7. Contains 1 note-duration pairs and 1 inline instrument selections. At the final opcode the interpreter repeats the pattern while repetitions remain. Otherwise it advances to the next cue pair.

SID pattern at $C394, selected by channel/pattern 3/8. Contains 2 note-duration pairs and 1 inline instrument selections. At the final opcode the interpreter repeats the pattern while repetitions remain. Otherwise it advances to the next cue pair.
Cue sequence at $C39A, used by channel/cue 4/12. Repeat count and pattern index pairs: 127×12. The high-bit byte ends the sequence.
Cue sequence at $C39D, used by channel/cue 4/13. Repeat count and pattern index pairs: 1×13. The high-bit byte ends the sequence.
Cue sequence at $C3A0, used by channel/cue 4/1. Repeat count and pattern index pairs: 1×0. The high-bit byte ends the sequence.
Cue sequence at $C3A3, used by channel/cue 4/11. Repeat count and pattern index pairs: 1×5. The high-bit byte ends the sequence.
Cue sequence at $C3A6, used by channel/cue 4/6. Repeat count and pattern index pairs: 1×5, 1×11. The high-bit byte ends the sequence.

SID pattern at $C3AA, selected by channel/pattern 4/5. Contains 15 note-duration pairs and 1 inline instrument selections. At the final opcode the interpreter repeats the pattern while repetitions remain. Otherwise it advances to the next cue pair.

SID pattern at $C3CA, selected by channel/pattern 4/11. Contains 4 note-duration pairs and 1 inline instrument selections. At the final opcode the interpreter repeats the pattern while repetitions remain. Otherwise it advances to the next cue pair.
Cue sequence at $C3D4, used by channel/cue 4/2. Repeat count and pattern index pairs: 1×1. The high-bit byte ends the sequence.

SID pattern at $C3D7, selected by channel/pattern 4/1. Contains 3 note-duration pairs and 1 inline instrument selections. At the final opcode the interpreter repeats the pattern while repetitions remain. Otherwise it advances to the next cue pair.
Cue sequence at $C3DF, used by channel/cue 3/6. Repeat count and pattern index pairs: 1×6. The high-bit byte ends the sequence.

SID pattern at $C3E2, selected by channel/pattern 3/6. Contains 3 note-duration pairs and 1 inline instrument selections. At the final opcode the interpreter repeats the pattern while repetitions remain. Otherwise it advances to the next cue pair.
Cue sequence at $C3EA, used by channel/cue 4/3. Repeat count and pattern index pairs: 1×2. The high-bit byte ends the sequence.
